the genetic configuration of a tumor cell determines its epigenetic profile.
the epigenome of a cancer cell is a reflection of its genetic makeup.
tumor-specific CpG island hypermethylated genes are not randomly distributed across the genome, and that they are not randomly selected from a pool of hypermethylated promoters.

the epigenetic silening of genes in human cancers, and the underlying mechanisms.
the epigenetic regulation of gene expression in normal and cancer cells and with the development and application of high-throughput techniques for the analysis of DNA methylation patterns.
the epigenetic regulation of the genome, with a particular emphasis on the epigenetic control of gene expression in normal and malignant cells.

CpG island methlyation is a consequence of genetic changes, not the cause of cancer.

the epigenetic signature in a tumor is driven by the genetic alterations that have occurred in the tumor cells, but that the epigenetics is not the cause of the genetic alterations, but rather the consequence of them.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the genetic configuration of the tumor cell is a driving factor of the CpG island methyliation signature.
the genetic configuration of a tumor is the main determinant of the CpG island hypermethylated phenotype.
DNA hypermethylation is a common epgenetic alteration associated with human cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the genetic configuration of a tumor cell determines its epigenetic signature, which in turn is associated with specific transcriptional profiles and tumor progression.
epigenetic alterations are not random, but rather are highly specific for each tumor type and reflect the genetic configuration of each tumor cell.
the epigenome of cancer cells is not random but rather reflects the genetic configuration of the cells.
